checks.claim: Applying Lemma J.1 in this weighted form gives
checks.explanation: A bias–variance decomposition must use the same weights as the cost being decomposed. Appendix J uses transport weights $T_{ij}$ but substitutes arithmetic cluster moments. Uniform row and column marginals do not make a column's weights uniform within each cluster, so the omitted centered cross term need not vanish.
checks.demonstration:
Take four unit visual vectors
$$v_1=(1,0),\quad v_2=(-1,0),\quad v_3=(\cos0.1,\sin0.1),\quad v_4=(0,1),$$
with clusters $\mathcal C_p=\{1,2\}$ and $\mathcal C_q=\{3,4\}$. Use the orthonormal subspace vectors $o_1=(1,0)$ and $o_2=(0,1)$. Define the balanced transport plan by
$$T_{\cdot1}=(0.249,0.001,0.249,0.001)^\top,\qquad T_{i2}=0.25-T_{i1}.$$
Every entry is positive, each row has mass $0.25$, and each column has mass $0.5$. Each cluster contributes mass $0.25$ to column one, so the theorem's positive mixed-cluster premise holds.

Write $c=\cos0.1$ and $s=\sin0.1$. The arithmetic moments are
$$\mu_p=(0,0),\quad \sigma_p^2=1,\qquad \mu_q=(c/2,(1+s)/2),\quad \sigma_q^2=(1-s)/2.$$
In particular, the centroids are distinct. The actual column-one cost is
$$C_1=\sum_{i=1}^4T_{i1}\|v_i-o_1\|^2=0.006+0.498(1-c)=0.00848792569\ldots.$$
With masses $\alpha_p=\beta_q=1/4$, the proposed lower bound instead equals
$$B_1=\alpha_p\sigma_p^2+\beta_q\sigma_q^2+\frac{\alpha_p\beta_q}{\alpha_p+\beta_q}\|\mu_p-\mu_q\|^2=\frac{7-s}{16}=0.43126041146\ldots.$$
Thus $C_1<B_1$, contradicting Eq. (10). Column weights concentrate near $v_1$ and $v_3$, both close to $o_1$; the arithmetic moments give equal weight to the nearly untransported $v_2$ and $v_4$ and cannot describe this cost.

Using column-weighted moments gives the valid lower bound $0.00711457706\ldots$, with nonnegative remainder $0.00137334863\ldots$, whose sum is the actual cost. Nor is the failure confined to this freely chosen feasible plan: the positive Sinkhorn plan for the same cosine costs with regularization $\lambda=0.01$ has column-one squared-distance cost $0.00249791736\ldots$, still below the arithmetic-moment bound $0.43126041146\ldots$.
checks.repair:
For a fixed column $j$, use its transport weights to define each positive cluster mass and its moments:
$$a_{k,j}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}T_{ij},\qquad \mu_{k,j}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}T_{ij}v_i}{a_{k,j}},$$
$$\sigma_{k,j}^2=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}T_{ij}\|v_i-\mu_{k,j}\|^2}{a_{k,j}}.$$
Weighted centering makes $\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}T_{ij}(v_i-\mu_{k,j})=0$, so
$$\sum_{i\in\mathcal C_k}T_{ij}\|v_i-o_j\|^2=a_{k,j}\sigma_{k,j}^2+a_{k,j}\|\mu_{k,j}-o_j\|^2.$$
For two clusters, completing the square in the last two terms gives the lower bound
$$a_{p,j}\sigma_{p,j}^2+a_{q,j}\sigma_{q,j}^2+\frac{a_{p,j}a_{q,j}}{a_{p,j}+a_{q,j}}\|\mu_{p,j}-\mu_{q,j}\|^2.$$
The omitted remainder is $(a_{p,j}+a_{q,j})\|o_j-\bar\mu_j\|^2\ge0$, where $\bar\mu_j$ is the mass-weighted mean of the two column centroids. This proves the corrected fixed-plan inequality, including for unit-norm $o_j$. Arithmetic moments would also be valid if weights were uniform within each cluster. Neither correction proves that optimizing a balanced plan eliminates mixing: in the weighted version the moments themselves change with $T$. The conclusion is therefore a lower bound for a fixed transport plan.
checks.scope: The defect concerns Eq. (10) and its moment decomposition. The corrected statement is a fixed-plan lower bound, rather than a guarantee that an optimal plan avoids mixing. The empirical anomaly-detection results are not assessed.

checks.claim: A nonempty river neighborhood contains every radius6gmax/gamma ball around the river while all gradients there are bounded by gmax and sharp curvature varies only very slowly.
checks.explanation: At a river point, the gradient has no component in a sharp Hessian direction. Moving in that direction initially increases the corresponding gradient component at a rate above $\gamma$. The third-derivative bound prevents the curvature from dropping fast enough to keep the gradient below $g_{\max}$ throughout the required ball. The premises are therefore inconsistent in their nondegenerate regime.
checks.demonstration:
Suppose the river $\mathcal M$ is nonempty, choose $w\in\mathcal M$, and work in the stated nondegenerate regime $d\ge2$, $\gamma>0$ and $g_{\max}>0$. Let $u$ be a unit sharp Hessian eigenvector at $w$. The river gradient is aligned with the flat eigenvector, so
$$u^\top\nabla L(w)=0,\qquad u^\top\nabla^2L(w)u>\gamma.$$
Set $r=2g_{\max}/\gamma$. The whole segment $w+tu$, $0\le t\le r$, lies strictly inside the ball of radius $6g_{\max}/\gamma$ required to be contained in $\mathcal U$.

Throughout this segment, Assumption 2.2 bounds the third-derivative operator norm by $\kappa\gamma^2/(2g_{\max})$. Therefore the sharp directional curvature obeys
$$u^\top\nabla^2L(w+tu)u>\gamma-\frac{\kappa\gamma^2}{2g_{\max}}t.$$
Integrating from zero to $r$ gives
$$u^\top\nabla L(w+ru)>r\gamma-\frac{r^2\kappa\gamma^2}{4g_{\max}}=(2-\kappa)g_{\max}.$$
The parameter restrictions imply $\kappa\le200^{-32}<1$. Hence
$$\|\nabla L(w+ru)\|>g_{\max},$$
contradicting the uniform gradient bound on $\mathcal U$.

Thus no nonempty river satisfies all the printed assumptions in this regime. Setting parameters to zero leaves the displayed conditions undefined, because of their divisions or normalized river gradient; at $d=1$ the printed sharp-eigenvalue index is also undefined. This is an inconsistency of the premises, not a landscape violating a conditional tracking theorem.
checks.repair:
Decouple the required neighborhood radius from the sharp-curvature and gradient bounds. A narrower tube makes the remaining conditions consistent. For example, take
$$L(x,y)=x^2-y,\qquad \mathcal M=\{0\}\times\mathbb R,\qquad \mathcal U=(-1/5,1/5)\times\mathbb R,$$
with $\gamma=1$, $\gamma_{\max}=200$, $g_{\max}=2$, $\kappa=200^{-40}$ and $\gamma_{\rm flat}=\kappa$. Every radius-$1/10$ ball around the river lies in this tube. Its gradient is $(2x,-1)$, with norm below two throughout $\mathcal U$; its Hessian eigenvalues are two and zero. The third derivative and flat-eigenvector derivative vanish. Gradient alignment with the flat eigenvector $(0,-1)$ occurs exactly at $x=0$, so the uniqueness condition holds as well.

This proves consistency after replacing the required radius, not the tracking or momentum theorem. For these constants the original required radius would be twelve. Appendix C.3.1 and later lemmas use neighborhoods proportional to $g_{\max}/\gamma$, so containment and tracking arguments must be proved again for any revised radius assumption.
checks.scope: Assumptions 2.1–2.2 define an empty model class in the regime used by the analysis. The conditional theorems are therefore vacuous there, rather than disproved. The construction is not a counterexample to momentum acceleration.
checks.whyItMatters: The formal tracking and acceleration results have no nonempty landscape to which they apply under the stated nondegenerate assumptions. A consistent geometric setting is needed before those results can describe training behavior.
checks.claimContext: Assumption 2.2 requires a large ball around every river point while bounding the gradient throughout that neighborhood. Its sharp-curvature and third-derivative conditions force a gradient larger than the bound before reaching the ball's boundary.
